Rank order is EVIDENCE-LED: the prolapse edge is first because it is the mechanism the located literature most consistently names, the anaemia edge is second because it has a cohort anchor and a severe case but a conflicting paediatric null, and the stricture edge is third because it is a SINGLE-CASE anchor whose own authors call the complication rare.

DIRECTION GUARD, APPLIED TO THE PROLAPSE EDGE: the located evidence reads mucosal prolapse as a CONTRIBUTING FACTOR TO this identity, and no located anchor studies prolapse as an outcome of established ulcer disease. That edge therefore registers a documented co-occurrence and a mechanistic coupling, NOT a secondary-condition consequence, and its associationBasis says so on its face.

CATEGORY-BOUNDARY GUARD, APPLIED TO ALL THREE EDGES: two of the located anchors diagnose MUCOSAL PROLAPSE SYNDROME, a broader descriptive category that both contains and is used less precisely than this catalog identity, and this catalog resolves them differently. Any individual claim must document which of the two entities was actually diagnosed.

No magnitude is stated for any edge. The prolapse edge has no co-occurrence rate. The anaemia edge carries conflicting anchors, an adult cohort that reports no anaemia rate within its 17 cases, a single transfusion-requiring case, and a paediatric series in which none of 12 patients had significant anaemia. The stricture edge is a single case whose own authors describe the complication as rare.

nexusClaim.associationBasis: Mucosal prolapse is the mechanism most often invoked for solitary rectal ulcer syndrome, and the located evidence repeatedly describes prolapse as the underlying process rather than as a separate disease. A comprehensive narrative review of solitary rectal ulcer syndrome states that the aetiology REMAINS UNCLEAR but lists contributing factors including MUCOSAL PROLAPSE, ischemia, paradoxical puborectalis contraction and digital trauma, and further notes that the disorder is frequently misdiagnosed as inflammatory bowel disease or rectal malignancy (PMID 42149300). A case of the syndrome presenting as simultaneous contralateral KISSING RECTAL ULCERS in an HIV-positive patient found histopathology demonstrating the characteristic triad of fibromuscular obliteration of the lamina propria, smooth muscle extension between distorted crypts and muscularis mucosae hypertrophy, ESTABLISHING OCCULT INTERNAL MUCOSAL PROLAPSE AS THE UNDERLYING MECHANISM, in the absence of any visible mucosal prolapse (PMID 42713425). A paediatric case of mucosal prolapse syndrome presenting with painless rectal bleeding and four rectal polyps initially attributed to Peutz-Jeghers syndrome was only reclassified as mucosal prolapse syndrome on repeat colonoscopy with biopsies a year later, and the authors report that the MORPHOLOGIC SIMILARITY BETWEEN HAMARTOMATOUS POLYP AND MUCOSAL PROLAPSE HISTOLOGY is itself a source of diagnostic error (PMID 38756112). Recorded as documented association only, and recorded in BOTH DIRECTIONS, because the located evidence reads prolapse as a contributor to the ulcer rather than the ulcer as a consequence of prolapse, which is stated openly below.
nexusClaim.causationStatus: Neither causation nor aggravation is established in either direction, and DIRECTION IS THE CENTRAL LIMITATION OF THIS EDGE: the located evidence describes mucosal prolapse as a CONTRIBUTING FACTOR TO solitary rectal ulcer syndrome, and NONE of the three anchors studies prolapse as an outcome or a consequence of established ulcer disease. This edge therefore registers a documented co-occurrence and a mechanistic coupling, NOT a secondary-condition consequence, and the associationBasis is written to make that direction explicit rather than to imply that the ulcer produces the prolapse. The primary anchor states plainly that the aetiology REMAINS UNCLEAR, so even the prolapse-to-ulcer direction is described as a contributing factor rather than a demonstrated cause. The second anchor is a SINGLE CASE whose decisive finding is the absence of visible prolapse at endoscopy, so it demonstrates that prolapse can be OCCULT and histologically inferred; it cannot establish frequency, and it is the located reason the mechanism claim names internal mucosal prolapse rather than visible descent. The third anchor concerns MUCOSAL PROLAPSE SYNDROME, a broader descriptive category that both contains and is used less precisely than solitary rectal ulcer syndrome, and it is a single paediatric case in which the initial diagnosis was wrong, so it contributes to the diagnostic-overlap problem rather than to any prevalence statement. Two of the three anchors therefore rest on a category boundary that this catalog resolves differently, and the target identity rectal-prolapse had ZERO registered incoming edges before this batch. Individual claims require a dated defecation history with straining, digitation and obstructed-defecation symptoms documented, a documented rectal examination and imaging or manometric assessment of descent, endoscopic evidence of mucosal changes, and histopathology showing the fibromuscular obliteration pattern, with a clinical determination separating prolapse from inflammatory bowel disease, from neoplasia and from habitual digitation.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: The hypothesised vector is chronic mechanical trauma from a dyssynergic defecation posture: repeated straining against a paradoxically contracting or poorly relaxing puborectalis, sometimes compounded by repeated digital evacuation, produces downward mucosal displacement and shearing of the rectal wall against itself, so the mucosa is pushed into the lumen, its blood supply is compromised by the compression, and the resulting ischaemia and friction produce the ulceration that the histologic triad of fibromuscular obliteration, smooth muscle extension between distorted crypts and muscularis mucosae hypertrophy records; the vector is named as the mechanical and pressure vector rather than as an inflammatory or vascular one because the located anchors describe a mechanism of repeated pressure and displacement and none attributes the ulcer to an immune or infectious process.

evidentiaryProfile.conservativeRationale: Authored at ASSOCIATION_ONLY at comprehensive-narrative-review, single-case-histopathological-report and single-case-diagnostic-redescription class, following the file's existing gastrointestinal and motility pathway scope. The narrative review is the anchor that states the aetiology is unclear and lists mucosal prolapse among the contributing factors, which is the located basis for the entire edge and for its refusal to assert a direction (PMID 42149300). The kissing-ulcer case is registered because it is the located source that establishes that the prolapse can be OCCULT and histologically inferred in the absence of visible descent, which is the specific finding that the mechanism claim depends on and that a claim built only on visible prolapse would miss (PMID 42713425). The paediatric case is registered as the located evidence that mucosal prolapse syndrome and solitary rectal ulcer syndrome are confused with one another and with other diagnoses, which is what makes the category-boundary disclosure on this edge necessary rather than optional (PMID 38756112). Because all three anchors either state the aetiology is unclear or are single cases, and because the direction supported by the evidence is the reverse of the direction this edge would nominally assert, the conservative standard holds the edge at association only with no magnitude.
evidentiaryProfile.evidenceGaps: DIRECTION IS THE CENTRAL LIMITATION: the located evidence reads mucosal prolapse as a CONTRIBUTING FACTOR TO solitary rectal ulcer syndrome, and NO located anchor studies prolapse as an outcome of established ulcer disease, so this edge registers a documented co-occurrence and a mechanistic coupling rather than a secondary-condition consequence (PMID 42149300, PMID 42713425, PMID 38756112). THE PRIMARY ANCHOR STATES THAT THE AETIOLOGY REMAINS UNCLEAR, describing prolapse as one contributing factor among ischemia, paradoxical puborectalis contraction and digital trauma, and so even the supported direction is not a demonstrated cause (PMID 42149300). TWO OF THE THREE ANCHORS REST ON A CATEGORY BOUNDARY THIS CATALOG RESOLVES DIFFERENTLY: the kissing-ulcer case turns on the diagnosis of MUCOSAL PROLAPSE SYNDROME or internal mucosal prolapse, and the paediatric case is a diagnosis of MUCOSAL PROLAPSE SYNDROME, a broader descriptive category that both contains and is used less precisely than this catalog identity, and neither reports a solitary rectal ulcer syndrome prevalence (PMID 42713425, PMID 38756112). BOTH OF THOSE ANCHORS ARE SINGLE CASES, and the paediatric one had an INCORRECT INITIAL DIAGNOSIS of Peutz-Jeghers syndrome that was corrected only on repeat biopsy a year later, so it evidences diagnostic confusion rather than any prevalence (PMID 38756112). NO located anchor reports how often prolapse is present in this identity, how often it is visible rather than occult, or how often the two conditions are treated together, and no located anchor separates the contribution of the prolapse from that of the dyssynergia or of habitual digitation.
alternativeEtiologiesToRuleOut: Habitual digital rectal evacuation, which the primary anchor names as an independent contributing factor and which can produce the same mucosal changes without any prolapse at all
Paradoxical puborectalis contraction or anismus, which the primary anchor names as a separate contributing factor and which requires manometric or imaging confirmation to distinguish from prolapse
Inflammatory bowel disease, which the primary anchor names as the most frequent misdiagnosis and which produces rectal ulceration through a wholly different mechanism
Rectal malignancy, which the primary anchor also names as a common misdiagnosis and which must be excluded histologically before this edge is applied

Instrumentation trauma, including the electric bidet and other repeated local trauma, which is a reported cause of severe circumferential rectal ulceration and is a further mechanical route independent of prolapse

sourceReferences.note: Comprehensive narrative review of solitary rectal ulcer syndrome covering clinical, endoscopic and histological features. The authors state that THE AETIOLOGY REMAINS UNCLEAR, with contributing factors such as MUCOSAL PROLAPSE, ischemia, paradoxical puborectalis contraction and digital trauma; diagnosis requires history, digital rectal examination, endoscopy, histopathology and physiological studies; treatment comprises lifestyle modification, biofeedback, topical agents, sclerotherapy and surgical intervention for refractory cases, with ongoing surveillance especially in patients at high risk of recurrence and individualised multidisciplinary management particularly in patients with psychiatric comorbidities or during pregnancy. Registered as the located basis for the whole edge AND as the anchor that establishes the direction limitation, since it names prolapse as a contributing factor to the ulcer and does not study prolapse as a consequence.

nexusClaim.associationBasis: Solitary rectal ulcer syndrome is a recognised benign cause of rectal bleeding and of iron-deficiency anaemia, and the located evidence spans a bleeding cohort, a severe transfusion-requiring case and a paediatric series that reports the opposite. In a tertiary-care series of 257 patients presenting with lower gastrointestinal bleeding, aged 15 to 70, SOLITARY RECTAL ULCER SYNDROME WAS FOUND IN 17 PATIENTS, 6.6 PERCENT, with perirectal bleeding, constipation, mucous discharge, abdominal pain AND ANAEMIA among the common clinical findings, and with obliterated lamina propria with collagen, ulceration, crypt distortion and inflammatory infiltrates as the common histological findings (PMID 36968942). A case of RECURRENT IRON DEFICIENCY ANAEMIA DUE TO MUCOSAL PROLAPSE SYNDROME described a 36-year-old man whose initial endoscopy, colonoscopy and capsule endoscopy showed no abnormality other than rectal mucosal prolapse syndrome without notable bleeding, who nine months later despite oral iron therapy developed bloody stools and SEVERE ANAEMIA AT A HAEMOGLOBIN OF 6.2 G/DL REQUIRING TRANSFUSION, and who remained symptom-free after transanal lumpectomy (PMID 40270668). AGAINST THAT, a prospective series of 12 consecutive children with solitary rectal ulcer syndrome reported that ALL CASES HAD NORMAL GROWTH and NONE HAD ANY EVIDENCE OF A BLEEDING DIATHESIS, SIGNIFICANT ANAEMIA, bacterial or parasitic infection or any other systemic disease to explain their bleeding, and the review literature places the adult incidence at approximately one in 100,000 (PMID 18188027). Recorded as documented association only, with the conflicting paediatric null carried openly.
nexusClaim.causationStatus: Neither causation nor aggravation is established for any individual, and THE THREE ANCHORS DISAGREE ON HOW OFTEN ANAEMIA OCCURS, which is stated rather than resolved. The primary anchor lists anaemia among common clinical findings but reports NO ANAEMIA RATE within its 17 solitary rectal ulcer syndrome cases, so a claim cannot attach a frequency to that list. The second anchor is a SINGLE CASE in which transfusion-requiring anaemia is the headline of the report, so it establishes that severe anaemia is possible and that it can be the presenting or late feature, and it establishes nothing about how often. The third anchor is a direct COUNTERWEIGHT: in 12 consecutive paediatric patients, NONE had significant anaemia, and the authors attribute their series' apparent rarity considerations to traditional squatting defecation rather than to haematological status. The population differences are substantial and unaddressed by any located anchor, because a paediatric cohort in a region with traditional squatting defecation cannot be compared with an adult bleeding cohort, and the primary anchor's 6.6 percent is a proportion of patients who PRESENTED WITH BLEEDING rather than a proportion of all patients with the syndrome. Individual claims require a dated bleeding history with the volume and duration documented, serial haemoglobin and iron studies with the transfusion history recorded, an assessment excluding an independent source of gastrointestinal blood loss, endoscopic confirmation of the rectal lesion with biopsy, and a clinical determination separating anaemia attributable to this lesion from anaemia due to co-existing gastric antral vascular ectasia, peptic ulceration, inflammatory bowel disease, malignancy or dietary iron deficiency.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: The hypothesised vector is chronic mucosal blood loss with impaired haeme-dependent mucosal healing: repeated or prolonged bleeding from an ulcerated and friable rectal mucosa, sustained straining at defecation and repeated local trauma keep the lesion open, so ongoing fractional blood loss depletes iron stores faster than intake replaces them, and the resulting iron-deficiency anaemia compounds the fatigue and reduced activity that in turn worsen the defecation dynamics that perpetuate the lesion; the vector is named as the blood-loss-plus-healing-demand mechanism rather than as a haematological or nutritional one because the located anchors describe a bleeding source and an iron-deficiency picture and do not attribute the anaemia to a marrow, renal or endocrine cause.

evidentiaryProfile.conservativeRationale: Authored at ASSOCIATION_ONLY at non-probability-convenience-sampled-prospective-cohort, single-transfusion-requiring-case-report and prospective-paediatric-case-series class, following the file's existing gastrointestinal and haematological pathway scope. The bleeding cohort is the anchor that establishes the syndrome as a recognised cause of lower gastrointestinal bleeding in adults and that places anaemia among the common clinical findings, with the 6.6 percent figure explicitly labelled as a proportion of patients who PRESENTED WITH BLEEDING (PMID 36968942). The case report is registered because it is the located source that establishes the extreme end of the range, recurrent iron deficiency anaemia progressing to a haemoglobin of 6.2 g/dl requiring transfusion despite oral iron, and its single-case nature is disclosed (PMID 40270668). The paediatric series is registered and NOT omitted because it is the located counterweight, twelve consecutive children with none having significant anaemia, and recording it is what keeps the edge from reading as a universal claim; its own explanation, that traditional squatting defecation may account for local recognition, is a population difference the edge cannot control for (PMID 18188027). Because the anchors disagree across populations and one is a single case, the conservative standard holds the edge at association only and refuses to state a magnitude.
evidentiaryProfile.evidenceGaps: THE ANCHORS DISAGREE ON FREQUENCY AND THE DISAGREEMENT IS UNRESOLVED: a 257-patient adult bleeding cohort lists anaemia among common findings but reports NO ANAEMIA RATE within its 17 syndrome cases, a single case reports transfusion-requiring anaemia, and a 12-patient paediatric series reports that NONE had significant anaemia (PMID 36968942, PMID 40270668, PMID 18188027). THE PRIMARY ANCHOR'S 6.6 PERCENT IS A PROPORTION OF PATIENTS WHO PRESENTED WITH LOWER GASTROINTESTINAL BLEEDING, NOT OF ALL PATIENTS WITH THE SYNDROME, so it is a presentation proportion and not a complication rate (PMID 36968942). THE SECOND ANCHOR IS A SINGLE CASE whose entire report concerns the anaemia, so it establishes that severe anaemia is possible and supports no frequency statement (PMID 40270668). THE THIRD ANCHOR IS PEDIATRIC and its authors attribute their series' findings partly to traditional squatting defecation, so the population differs from the adult bleeding cohort in a way no located anchor controls for; it is registered as a counterweight rather than as contradicting evidence to be discarded (PMID 18188027). THE SECOND ANCHOR'S DIAGNOSIS IS MUCOSAL PROLAPSE SYNDROME rather than this catalog identity, a broader category that this catalog resolves differently, and its initial endoscopy, colonoscopy and capsule endoscopy showed NO notable bleeding at all before the severe anaemia developed nine months later, so the bleeding-to-anaemia interval is unobserved (PMID 40270668). NO located anchor reports an iron-study profile, a transfusion rate, a haemoglobin distribution, or the proportion of syndrome patients who are anaemic at presentation, and no located anchor excludes a second concurrent bleeding source in any of its cases, one of which is explicitly a co-existing gastric antral vascular ectasia case.
alternativeEtiologiesToRuleOut: A second concurrent bleeding source, and in one located anchor it is explicit, since gastric antral vascular ectasia was the co-diagnosed cause of the same anaemia and would on its own account for a substantial fraction of any haemoglobin deficit

Co-existing peptic ulceration, inflammatory bowel disease or colorectal malignancy, all of which present with lower gastrointestinal bleeding and all of which are missed in a substantial share of patients whose bleeding is attributed to a benign rectal lesion
Dietary iron deficiency, chronic blood loss from other sources, and reduced intake during a chronic painful illness, any of which can produce iron-deficiency anaemia without any rectal lesion
Chronic kidney disease, thalassaemia trait and anaemia of chronic disease, which produce anaemia by wholly different mechanisms and which must be excluded before the edge is applied to an individual
Haemorrhoids and anal fissure, which are far more common sources of rectal bleeding and are frequently present alongside this lesion without being the cause of the anaemia

SOLITARY RECTAL ULCER SYNDROME WAS FOUND IN 17 PATIENTS, 6.6 PERCENT, with 57 PERCENT male. Perirectal bleeding, constipation, mucous discharge, abdominal pain AND ANAEMIA were the common clinical findings; solitary lesions, ulceration and anterior rectum location the common endoscopic findings; obliterated lamina propria with collagen, ulceration, crypt distortion and inflammatory infiltrates the common histological findings. sourceReferences.note: Single case of SEVERE ANAEMIA DUE TO MUCOSAL PROLAPSE SYNDROME REQUIRING BLOOD TRANSFUSION. A 36-year-old man was referred for recurrent iron deficiency anaemia; initial oesophagogastroduodenoscopy, colonoscopy and capsule endoscopy revealed no significant abnormality other than rectal mucosal prolapse syndrome WITHOUT NOTABLE BLEEDING; nine months later, despite oral iron therapy, he developed bloody stools and severe anaemia at a haemoglobin of 6.2 g/dl requiring transfusion; repeat colonoscopy showed an enlarged mucosal prolapse, transanal lumpectomy was performed, and he remained symptom-free thereafter. The authors conclude clinicians should remain vigilant about the potential for severe anaemia requiring transfusion. Registered because it establishes the extreme end of the range. DISCLOSED: a SINGLE CASE, and its diagnosis is MUCOSAL PROLAPSE SYNDROME, a broader category than this catalog identity, with the bleeding-to-anaemia interval unobserved because the initial endoscopy showed no bleeding.

nexusClaim.associationBasis: Stricture formation is a described but uncommon consequence of the chronic fibrotic and ischaemic course of solitary rectal ulcer syndrome, and the located evidence consists of a single documented case with a full mechanistic account. A report of solitary rectal ulcer syndrome with FIBROTIC RECTAL STRICTURE in a 60-year-old patient sets out the pathogenesis as RECTAL WALL COMPRESSION, ISCHEMIA DUE TO POOR BLOOD SUPPLY, CHRONIC INFLAMMATION and MECHANICAL TRAUMA DUE TO REPEATED DIGITAL EVACUATION, leading to mucosal ulceration and, IN SOME CASES, FIBROSIS AND STRICTURE FORMATION; the authors state that STRICTURE IN THIS SYNDROME IS RARE and may MIMIC MALIGNANCY, leading to delays in appropriate diagnosis, that the differential includes inflammatory bowel disease and neoplasms, and that HISTOPATHOLOGICAL CONFIRMATION REMAINS THE GOLD STANDARD. Diagnosis in that case required colonoscopy, anorectal manometry, magnetic resonance defecography and histopathology, and management combined a high-fibre diet, laxatives, biofeedback therapy, argon plasma coagulation and DILATATION OF THE STRICTURE (PMID 40923374). Recorded as documented association only, and recorded as a SINGLE-ANCHOR EDGE, with the rarity stated by the anchor itself and carried openly.
nexusClaim.causationStatus: Neither causation nor aggravation is established for any individual, and THIS EDGE RESTS ON A SINGLE ANCHOR, which is the located case report of one 60-year-old patient. The anchor's authors state that stricture in this syndrome is RARE, so the edge exists to record a described possibility and NOT to assert that stricture is a common sequel, and no frequency is stated. The mechanism the anchor offers is a plausible composite of compression, ischemia, chronic inflammation and repeated mechanical trauma, and the anchor does not establish which of these four produced the fibrosis in its own patient. The anchor also states that stricture in this syndrome MIMICS MALIGNANCY, which means a proportion of any apparent stricture series may reflect diagnostic misclassification in either direction and that a stricture attributed to this syndrome requires positive histopathology rather than endoscopic appearance alone. The target identity, anorectal-stricture, is BROADER than the rectal stricture the anchor describes, and that widening is disclosed rather than hidden. Individual claims require a dated diagnosis of the syndrome with prior histopathological confirmation, a documented stricture on endoscopy or cross-sectional imaging, a biopsy of the stricture to exclude neoplasm and inflammatory bowel disease, a documented manometric and defecographic assessment of the underlying defecation disorder, and a clinical determination separating fibrotic stricture from neoplastic stenosis, from post-inflammatory stricture and from postsurgical or radiation stricture.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: The hypothesised vector is chronic ischaemic and mechanical injury resolving in fibrosis: repeated straining, paradoxically increased puborectalis tone, wall compression and repeated digital evacuation injure the rectal mucosa and compromise its microcirculation, and an ulcer that cycles through ischaemia, inflammation and re-epithelialisation over years heals by depositing collagen in the submucosa and muscular wall, so the compliant rectal lumen becomes narrowed and fixed; the vector is named as the ischaemic-and-repeated-trauma-to-fibrosis sequence rather than as a single inflammatory or neoplastic process because the anchor's own account is explicitly composite and does not isolate a single contributor.

evidentiaryProfile.conservativeRationale: Authored at ASSOCIATION_ONLY at single-case-report class, following the file's existing gastrointestinal, motility and treatment-related pathway scope. The case report is the sole anchor because it is the located source that both documents the stricture presentation and supplies its mechanistic account, and it is registered for those two functions together (PMID 40923374). The conservative standard holds the edge at association only, states the anchor's own rarity claim on the face of the edge, and refuses to state any magnitude, because a single case report of a complication its own authors describe as rare is the weakest class of evidence available for an edge and the only honest handling is to record it as a described possibility rather than to dress it as an established association. The broader-scope issue with the target identity, and the malignancy-mimic warning that the anchor itself raises, are recorded on the edge rather than in the note alone.

alternativeEtiologiesToRuleOut: Neoplastic stenosis, which the anchor names as the principal differential and which its own authors state is mimicked by this presentation, making histological exclusion mandatory rather than optional
Inflammatory bowel disease, named by the anchor as a differential and a recognised cause of anorectal stricture through a wholly different mechanism
Post-surgical, post-anaesthetic or radiation-induced anorectal stricture, which would produce narrowing in the same anatomical site without any ulcer syndrome
Chronic constipation with faecal impaction and inflammatory cap polyposis, which can narrow the lumen by a sustained mechanical and inflammatory route rather than by submucosal fibrosis
Ischaemic colitis, which the anchor names as part of the pathogenesis and which would independently produce stricturing and must be excluded on histology

sourceReferences.citation: Pranami A, Verma A, Dahale A, et al. Solitary Rectal Ulcer Syndrome with Fibrotic Rectal Stricture: A Diagnostic Dilemma. Ann Afr Med. 2026 Jul 1;25(4):1013-1016. doi: 10.4103/aam.aam_322_25. PMID 40923374.
sourceReferences.note: Single case report of SOLITARY RECTAL ULCER SYNDROME WITH FIBROTIC RECTAL STRICTURE in a 60-year-old patient, diagnosed with colonoscopy, anorectal manometry, magnetic resonance defecography and histopathology and managed with a high-fibre diet, laxatives, biofeedback therapy, argon plasma coagulation and DILATATION OF THE STRICTURE. The authors set out the pathogenesis as RECTAL WALL COMPRESSION, ischemia due to poor blood supply, chronic inflammation and MECHANICAL TRAUMA DUE TO REPEATED DIGITAL EVACUATION, leading to mucosal ulceration and, in some cases, FIBROSIS AND STRICTURE FORMATION; they state that STRICTURE IN THIS SYNDROME IS RARE, that it may MIMIC MALIGNANCY leading to delays in diagnosis, that the differential includes inflammatory bowel disease and neoplasms, and that HISTOPATHOLOGICAL CONFIRMATION REMAINS THE GOLD STANDARD. Registered as the sole anchor for this edge, for both the documented presentation and its mechanistic account. DISCLOSED: a SINGLE CASE, the anchor describes a RECTAL rather than anorectal stricture, and its mechanism is explicitly composite with no contributor isolated.

CONFLICTING ANCHORS CARRIED RATHER THAN RESOLVED: the anaemia edge registers an adult bleeding cohort that lists anaemia among common findings, a single case with transfusion-requiring anaemia at a haemoglobin of 6.2 g/dl, and a 12-patient paediatric series in which NONE had significant anaemia. The disagreement is stated on the face of the edge and the paediatric counterweight is retained deliberately.

SINGLE-ANCHOR EDGE DECLARED: the anorectal-stricture edge rests on one case report whose own authors describe the complication as rare and as mimicking malignancy. It is registered to record a described possibility and carries no magnitude, no frequency and no causal claim.
